column1: What are the three guarantees in the CAP theorem, and how many can a distributed system guarantee simultaneously during a partition?
column2: Consistency, Availability, and Partition tolerance — only two can be guaranteed simultaneously; since partitions are inevitable, the real choice is between C and A.

column1: Why must partition tolerance (P) be treated as non-negotiable in real-world microservice deployments?
column2: Because network failures (switch failures, cable disconnects, AZ outages) are routine operational realities, not theoretical edge cases, forcing architects to choose between C and A when a partition occurs.

column1: What is a Bounded Context in Domain-Driven Design?
column2: A linguistic boundary within which a single, unambiguous model of a domain concept applies; the same real-world entity (e.g., 'Product') can have entirely different, valid models in different bounded contexts.

column1: What is a Context Map in DDD, and why is it necessary?
column2: An explicit translation contract defined at the boundary between bounded contexts, allowing services with different internal models of the same concept to communicate without forcing a shared, ambiguous God Object.

column1: What is temporal coupling, and why is it considered the most insidious coupling dimension in distributed systems?
column2: Temporal coupling occurs when two components must be simultaneously available for either to do useful work (e.g., a synchronous REST call); it is insidious because it directly ties service availability and latency together, propagating failures across the call chain.

column1: What is the core tradeoff between synchronous (REST/gRPC) and asynchronous (queue/pub-sub) inter-service communication?
column2: Synchronous protocols create temporal coupling (caller blocks, latency compounds, failures cascade), while asynchronous messaging decouples services in time at the cost of eventual consistency windows and harder request-response correlation.

column1: Why can't two independent databases (e.g., PostgreSQL for Orders, MySQL for Inventory) participate in a single ACID transaction?
column2: They do not share a WAL, lock manager, or commit log — they are independent correctness universes; this is a direct consequence of CAP theorem physics, not a database-specific limitation.

column1: What does the BASE acronym stand for, and what problem does it solve?
column2: Basically Available, Soft state, Eventually consistent — it is the operationally honest alternative to ACID for distributed systems that choose availability over strict consistency, allowing observable intermediate states (e.g., 'inventory reserved but payment pending').

column1: What is the precise meaning of 'eventual consistency' as a liveness guarantee?
column2: Given no further updates, all replicas will converge to the same value within a bounded time window — it is not merely 'eventually correct if lucky,' but a bounded, observable convergence guarantee.

column1: What are the three pillars of the observability triad, and what does each uniquely provide?
column2: Metrics (aggregate statistical health signals for alerting/capacity planning), Logs (discrete per-service event detail for forensic analysis), and Traces (reconstructed cross-service causal graphs linking requests across hops).

column1: Why does a traditional stack trace fail in a microservices architecture, and what replaces it?
column2: Execution state is distributed across autonomous processes with independent address spaces and asynchronous communication, so a single contiguous call stack doesn't exist; it is replaced by a distributed trace reconstructed from correlation IDs propagated through request headers.

column1: What is the 'declarative state reconciliation loop,' and why is it more robust than imperative deployment scripts?
column2: It is a level-triggered control loop that continuously observes actual runtime state, compares it to desired state, and drives convergence via corrective actions; it is more robust because transient failures (crashes, OOM kills, partitions) don't leave the system in an undefined state requiring manual fixes, unlike linear imperative scripts.
